P1.evidence: The prior conversation was acknowledged but not read back — the rep actually disclosed the opposite: 'I know you were speaking a bit with Kim ... He didn't give me a ton of info about you, so might ask you a few of the same questions that he might have asked.' That is the reverse of making the prospect feel seen. No frame of any kind was set — none of the four parts, and no 'does that work?'. The rep went straight from introductions to the open question, which did run: 'really just want to understand what's going on with your fitness right now. What are you looking to do?'

P2.evidence: Age, height and weight were all volunteered unprompted in the opening minutes — 'I'm about, like, 135 pounds', 'I'm about 5'10"', 'I am young. I'm 23 years old' — and the rep never asked for any of them, which scores as a miss. Work was explored usefully ('So you guys have like a store or an e-com store?') and the schedule problem surfaced, but never the sedentary-versus-on-feet question. Health was asked once, framed as motivation rather than screening: 'Is there any like, things going on with your health right now, which has got you wanting to prioritize it?' — no hereditary question. Injuries, chronic pain and movement limitations were never raised at all, which matters because the prospect is a boulderer being moved onto loaded ballistic work. Results from current training ran well: 'Why do you feel like, with what you're doing, with your routine, you haven't gotten there yet?' Diet ran. Sleep was never asked despite the prospect volunteering he is a night owl who eats his first meal at 2-4pm; energy never came up.

P3.evidence: This is where the call was lost. Surface goals were gathered adequately via 'do you have any, let's say, tangible goals in the near future, let's say the next three, six, 12 months?' The bridge to the real driver was attempted once and in a leading, deflating form — 'Is it just for, like, I don't know, vanity, or do you have any other, you know, reasons why you're wanting to...' — the prospect said 'Not really, just want to just better myself, really. That's all', and the rep replied 'Yeah, that's just that' and moved on. No second attempt. 'What does that actually do for you', 'who else does that impact' and the drive through to identity, family or longevity never ran, so nothing emotional was ever established. Bouldering was mentioned four times and never used as the 'something you want to do but can't' hook. No reflect-back. The $6,000 then landed on an entirely surface-level foundation, which is exactly why 'I'd definitely say it was worth it, but it's just hard at this point right now to kind of fork out that money' had nothing underneath it to push against.

P4.evidence: Past attempts were approached obliquely — 'is this like the first time that you've reached out to anyone for guidance or anything?' and 'How long have you been working out for?' — which established there were no prior paid attempts, but never asked what he had tried and what happened. The root-cause question did run in useful form: 'Why do you feel like, with what you're doing, with your routine, you know, you haven't gotten there yet?' The gap was named by the prospect himself in response to a good question — 'what do you feel like you would be looking for from Trevor specifically?' → 'a better, yeah, like more structure, like a real plan, you know? Right now I'm kind of just doing whatever.' That is the strongest moment of the call and the rep did not build on it. 'The information isn't the problem — why can't you stick to it on your own?' never ran.

P5.evidence: Entirely absent. No two-year question, no 'willing to settle', no 'why not', no line in the sand. With a 23-year-old whose stated driver is 'just better myself', this phase was the only route to a cost of inaction, and it was skipped.

P6.evidence: No commitment check before the price. The nearest equivalent — 'would that be worth $6,000 or no?' — came after the number, as part of handling the money objection, which is the wrong order. 'Is there any reason you wouldn't go all in' never ran, so there was no verbal yes to hold him to when he asked to think about it.

P11.evidence: No close was attempted. Price was presented, three cheaper options followed, and the call ended on 'Definitely just gotta think about it a little more' / 'Yeah, man.' Payment, the Trevor onboarding call, the agreement and the welcome-email steps were never reached. Note that the manager had mandated the previous day that no follow-up goes on the calendar without a deposit; no deposit was asked for and no follow-up was booked.

objection_plays.detail: The best-run objection on either of this rep's calls in this batch, and still incomplete. Isolation was excellent and specific: 'are you saying it's expensive as in I don't have that much money available on hand or like I don't think it's worth that much?' The worth-it reframe ran and landed: 'if you added, let's say 10 pounds of muscle ... cutting the body fat percentage down, would that be worth $6,000 or no?' → 'Yeah, I'd definitely say it was.' Permission for the financial conversation was sought softly — 'you don't have to tell me exactly about, like, what is, like, the cash on hand' — and three good picture questions followed: whether business expenses run through his personal account, whether the money is half his brother's, and whether he pays himself a set salary. Credit cards, available credit and investments were never asked, and the 'HOW not SHOULD I' frame never ran. Then, when the prospect asked directly whether the price was firm, the rep conceded rather than held, producing three lower numbers in under three minutes.

'I would definitely have to think about that a little bit' at 00:28:30 and again at 00:34:38. The rep's one good instinct was the probe 'What part?', which produced a usable answer. After that none of the play ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you there', no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is'. The second time it surfaced the rep answered 'Yeah, man' and the call ended.

Script gap. Fifteen minutes before the price the prospect asked to buy a reduced-scope version — training only, no nutrition, for less money. There is no scripted play for a scope-reduction request. The rep handled it reasonably on instinct: he deferred it, then declined to unbundle ('we don't really subtract it and then lower the prices, it's just part of the process anyway') and reframed by suggesting the prospect's whole-food diet might still be wrong or insufficient, which the prospect accepted ('I think that's maybe something I do struggle with too'). Worth adding to the playbook as a proper play, because unbundling requests are a cheaper form of the price objection and arrive before the number.

notes: The commercial half of this call was handled better than the discovery half — the isolation question and the worth-it reframe were textbook — but it was built on nothing, because P3, P5 and P6 were all effectively skipped. Coach the single highest-leverage habit: when a prospect answers the 'what's really driving this' question with 'not really, just want to better myself', that is the moment to ask again a different way, not to say 'yeah, that's just that' and move on. Second, hold the price when asked if it is firm; conceding three tiers in three minutes taught this prospect that waiting produces a better number.
